strings.why.disclaimer: Benchmarks are general rules of thumb from the sources named. They are not financial advice and vary by country and situation.
strings.why.basis.avg: Average of your last {n} completed period(s)
strings.why.assumedNet: No gross income is set in Settings, so your recorded income (usually after tax) is used. Lenders use gross income, so this ratio reads higher than theirs.
strings.why.rule.none: Add some income and spending to see this.
strings.why.forecast.f:
Expected daily spending = your everyday spending after removing one-off purchases (now {daily} a day; a typical week is {week}).
Projected balance = today's cash + scheduled bills and income − expected spending.
The shaded band is the 80% range: expected spending ± 1.28 × your usual spread, growing with √days.
strings.why.health.f: Average of the four pillars in the Financial Health Report (Spend, Save, Borrow, Plan), each scored 0–100 from published benchmarks.
strings.why.xirr.f: Find the yearly rate r where the sum of cash flow ÷ (1 + r)^(days since the first flow ÷ 365) equals zero. Money you put in counts negative; money you take out, and today's value, count positive.
strings.why.loan.f:
Monthly interest = balance × APR ÷ 12.
Payment for a term = balance × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)^−months), where i = APR ÷ 12.
Each month interest is paid first; the rest of the payment reduces the balance.
strings.why.recurring.f: A payee is suggested when it repeats on a steady rhythm (weekly, every 2 weeks, monthly, quarterly or yearly) at least 3 times (2 for yearly), the gaps agree within a few days, and the amounts stay within about 35% of their median.
strings.why.networth.n: Foreign-currency accounts are converted with the exchange rates you typed in Settings. Penny also saves a snapshot every day, so the history chart shows real past values from now on.
strings.why.rule.n: Needs = categories marked Need (by default groceries, housing, utilities, transport, health, education); wants = everything else. Change a category's type when you edit it.
strings.why.dti.n: Counts the monthly payment you entered on each loan or credit account.
strings.why.forecast.n1: One-off purchases far above your usual amounts are left out of the daily estimate so one big buy does not distort the future. They are listed above.
strings.why.forecast.n2: With under 28 days of history the range is wide and confidence is low. Weekday patterns need 8+ weeks; yearly seasonality needs 13+ months.
strings.why.forecast.n3: This is a projection from your own history, not a prediction or advice.
strings.why.health.n: The same score as the Report. A summary for orientation only.
strings.why.xirr.n: Dividends and fees recorded on the account are part of the return; transfers in and out are the cash flows.
strings.why.xirr.short: Under 3 months of history: an annualised figure can be misleading.
strings.why.loan.n: Interest is rounded to the cent each month, like a lender's statement. Your lender's figures may differ slightly.
strings.why.recurring.n: Suggestions are never created automatically. You choose which ones to track.
strings.why.savings.b: Saving at least 20% of income is a common target.
strings.why.savings.s: 50/30/20 budgeting rule — Elizabeth Warren & Amelia Warren Tyagi, “All Your Worth” (2005)
strings.why.rule.b: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt repayment.
strings.why.rule.s: Elizabeth Warren & Amelia Warren Tyagi, “All Your Worth” (2005)
strings.why.emergency.b: Planners commonly suggest 3 to 6 months of essential expenses in cash. Penny uses 6 as the goal; one-income or irregular-pay households often aim for the high end.
strings.why.emergency.s: Common financial-planning guidance (a rule of thumb, not a regulation)
strings.why.dti.b: 36% or less of gross income going to all debt payments.
strings.why.dti.s: The traditional 28/36 lender guideline (a mortgage-underwriting rule of thumb; limits vary by lender and country)
strings.why.housing.b: 28% or less of gross income going to housing.
strings.why.housing.s: The traditional 28/36 lender guideline (a mortgage-underwriting rule of thumb; limits vary by lender and country)

strings.help.title: Help
strings.help.b.start: Add your accounts first (Accounts → New), then log spending with N or the + button. Penny works out balances, budgets and forecasts from what you enter.
strings.help.b.accounts: Each account has its own currency. Totals are converted into your main currency with the exchange rates you type in Settings → Language & money. If a rate is missing, Penny says so instead of guessing.
strings.help.b.tx: Use Split on the Add sheet to divide one receipt across categories; the parts must add up to the total. Penny asks before saving a date in the future or a likely duplicate.
strings.help.b.import: Transactions → Import accepts CSV, TSV, OFX and QFX. Check the columns and date order in the preview, skip duplicates, and use Undo if anything looks wrong. A safety backup is taken first.
strings.help.b.budgets: Set a monthly limit per category. Turn on carry-over to roll unspent money (or overspending) into the next month.
strings.help.b.health: Savings rate, 50/30/20, emergency fund, debt-to-income and housing ratio are measured over your last completed months. Tap the ? beside any number to see the formula, your inputs and the benchmark.
strings.help.b.forecast: The forecast uses your typical spending (the median, not the average), ignores one-off outliers, and shows an 80% range. It gets more reliable with more months of data.
strings.help.b.recurring: Penny finds repeating payments in your history and offers to turn them into bills. Bills and reminders can post automatically.
strings.help.b.backup: Penny keeps automatic backups. To move to a new PC, export a copy from Settings → Data & backups and import it there.
strings.help.b.privacy: Your data is one encrypted file on this PC and is never uploaded. On Windows it is encrypted with AES-256 and locked to your Windows account; set a passcode to add a second lock and get a recovery key.
strings.help.b.trouble: Every bulk change and import has an Undo. You can restore any automatic backup from Settings → Data & backups, and open the log folder to share with support.

strings.rp.sub: Built from your numbers and published research, nothing leaves this PC
strings.rp.subEmpty: An evidence-based reading of your money

strings.rp.pillarsTitle: Four pillars: Spend, Save, Borrow, Plan
strings.rp.pillarsBody: Penny’s own reading, scored 0 to 100 from the benchmarks below. It is not a credit score and not the Financial Health Network’s official score.
strings.rp.pillarsMissing: Some pillars are blank because the data they need is missing.
strings.rp.regionIntl: country-specific rules are marked or skipped
strings.rp.noPrioritiesD: Your numbers sit within the benchmarks Penny checks.
strings.rp.b.spendIncome: Spending below income is the base of every other goal.
strings.rp.b.rise: Compared with the average of your previous three periods.
strings.rp.b.rate: Aim for 10–20% of income. The 50/30/20 rule says 20%; Fidelity (US) suggests at least 15% for retirement.
strings.rp.b.buffer: Target {n} months of essentials (3 to 6 months is the usual range).
strings.rp.b.bufferVol: Target {n} months of essentials; your income is {level} (variation {cv}).
strings.rp.b.weeks: JPMorgan Chase Institute: about 6 weeks covered a typical income dip plus expense spike.
strings.rp.b.van: Having at least $2,000 saved was linked to a 21% higher financial well-being score (US study).
strings.rp.b.dtiUS: US lender convention: keep total debt payments at or below 36%.
strings.rp.b.dti: Many lenders cap total debt payments at about 30–40% of income; the exact limit depends on your country.
strings.rp.n.grossEst: Gross income is estimated from take-home. Enter it in Settings for accuracy.
strings.rp.n.fx: Some accounts use a currency without an exchange rate and are left out.
strings.rp.b.fiTime: Starting from {start} invested, saving {save} a year, with {real} real return. A projection, not a promise.
strings.rp.n.needSavings: Needs income, spending and some savings.
strings.rp.act.starterI: {amount} to reach one month of essentials
strings.rp.act.starterW: Emergency savings were the strongest predictor of financial well-being in Vanguard’s survey, and the World Bank tracks the ability to cover an emergency as a core measure of financial health worldwide.
strings.rp.act.payDownI: Every {amount} paid off saves about {saved} a year in interest
strings.rp.act.payDownW: Highest-rate-first minimises interest. Cash sitting in savings earns far less than a card charges.
strings.rp.act.rateW: Common guidelines range from 15% to 20% of income; 10% is a realistic first step.
strings.rp.act.bufferVol: (the target is higher because your income is {level})
strings.rp.act.bufferW: Three to six months of essential spending is the common range; irregular income argues for the upper end.
strings.rp.act.dti: Bring debt payments under 36% of gross income
strings.rp.act.dtiW: Lenders treat about a third of income as a comfortable ceiling for total debt payments.
strings.rp.act.checkW: Spending that jumps above your own recent average is the cheapest place to find money.
strings.rp.act.strong: You are on a strong footing: put surplus to work
strings.rp.act.strongI: Keep saving; compare investing against your debts’ interest rates
strings.rp.act.strongW: Saving 15% or more of income, a funded buffer and no expensive debt is the position most retirement plans assume.
strings.rp.lab.never: At the minimum payments you entered, at least one debt never pays off. Raise the payment or add extra below.
strings.rp.lab.avaLess: Avalanche costs least in interest ({amount} less than snowball here).
strings.rp.lab.avaSame: Avalanche costs least in interest (about the same as snowball for your debts).
strings.rp.lab.research: Research finds that clearing one debt at a time keeps people motivated, so if the gap is small, the method you will stick with is a sound choice.
strings.rp.lab.needData: Enter the monthly payment and interest rate on each debt (Accounts, tap the debt) to compare payoff strategies.
strings.rp.howToRead: How to read this: benchmarks are rules of thumb from published studies. Several come from the US; where a rule depends on one country it is marked, and the dollar threshold is shown only for US dollars. Individual circumstances differ. Projections assume steady returns and do not include taxes, state pensions or social security. Penny is not a financial adviser; use this as a starting point for your own decisions or a conversation with a qualified professional. Everything is computed on this PC from your own data.
strings.rp.g.savingsD: The share of the money you received that you did not spend. If you earned 2,000 and spent 1,700, your savings rate is 15%.
strings.rp.g.bufferD: Money you can reach quickly, like cash and current or savings accounts, measured in months of essential spending. It keeps a surprise bill or a lost job from turning into debt.
strings.rp.g.essentialsD: Spending you can’t easily skip: housing, utilities, groceries, transport, insurance and minimum debt payments.
strings.rp.g.aprD: What a debt costs per year, as a percentage of what you owe. A card at 20% APR adds about 200 a year for every 1,000 you carry.
strings.rp.g.dtiD: Your monthly debt payments divided by your monthly income before tax. Lenders use it to judge how much more you can safely borrow.
strings.rp.g.networthD: Everything you own (accounts, savings, investments) minus everything you owe. Watching it rise over time matters more than its size today.
strings.rp.g.swrD: The share of your savings you could spend each year without running out. 4% is the classic rule; Morningstar’s 2026 estimate is 3.9%.
strings.rp.g.realD: Investment growth after inflation. If prices rise 3% and your investments grow 7%, the real return is about 4%.
strings.tour.welcome.d: A calm, private home for your money. Everything stays on this PC, encrypted, with no account and no cloud. Want a one-minute tour of the essentials?
strings.tour.overview.d: Net worth, what’s safe to spend today, your savings rate and upcoming bills, all on one screen.
strings.tour.add.d: Type it like you’d say it: “coffee 4.50 yesterday”. Penny fills in the amount, category and date.
strings.tour.ask.d: Jump to any page or ask “how much did I spend on food last month?”. Answers are worked out on this PC.
strings.tour.privacy.d: Blur every amount when someone is looking over your shoulder. Hover an amount to peek.
strings.tour.import.d: Import statements from your bank (CSV or OFX). Penny recognises most layouts and flags duplicates.
strings.tour.budgets.d: Set limits per category, or let Penny suggest them from your last three months.
strings.tour.reminders.d: Rent, bills, subscriptions: Penny sends a Windows notification on time, even from the tray.
strings.tour.report.d: Four simple pillars, clear priorities and a debt payoff planner, backed by published research. Save it as a PDF any time.
strings.tour.security.d: Your data is already encrypted. Add a passcode in Settings › Security for a second lock, plus a recovery key.
strings.tour.done.d: Start with one of these, or explore on your own. You can replay this tour any time from Settings or Ctrl K.
strings.tour.rowD: A one-minute walk-through of the main controls
strings.tour.security.d2: Add a passcode in Settings › Security to encrypt your data and lock Penny when you step away.

strings.in.allClear: Nothing needs your attention right now.
strings.in.welcome.d: Add a few transactions or import a bank statement, and Penny will start spotting patterns for you.
strings.in.cash.d: Your projected balance dips to {amount} around {date}. Move money or trim spending before then.
strings.in.payday.d: Your next income looks due on {date}. You have {cash} in cash, so you’re covered.
strings.in.payday.dShort: Your next income looks due on {date}, but you only have {cash} in cash. Plan ahead.
strings.in.dup.d: {amount} on {d1} and again on {d2}. Check whether both were intended.
strings.in.hike.d: {from} → {to}. That’s {year} more a year if it repeats monthly.
strings.in.spend.up.d: {now} so far vs {then} at the same point before.
strings.in.spend.down.d: {amount} less than at the same point before. Nice.
strings.in.rise.t: {name} rose three months in a row
strings.in.inc.down.d: {now} vs your usual {avg}. If it stays lower, Penny’s safe-to-spend will adjust.
strings.in.inc.up.d: {now} vs your usual {avg}. A good moment to top up a goal.
strings.in.goal.past.d: {amount} still to go. Pick a new date or a smaller target.
strings.in.goal.late.d: At your current pace it takes about {months} months (target: {target}). Putting aside {need} a month ({more} more) gets it there on time.
strings.in.goal.ok.d: {need} a month gets you there on time, and you’re saving enough to cover it.
strings.in.rate.good.d: Above the 20% rule of thumb. Fantastic.
strings.in.rate.neg.d: A gap of {amount} in this range.
strings.in.run.good.d: Your cash would cover 6+ months of normal spending. A strong safety net.
strings.in.run.low.d: Experts suggest 3–6 months of spending ({lo}–{hi}). A goal makes it easier.
strings.in.streak.d: Your best in the last 4 months is {best} days.
strings.in.nospend.d: Zero-spend days are the quietest way to boost savings.
strings.in.top.d: {amount}, {pct} of your spending in this range.
strings.in.subs.d: That’s {year} a year. Worth a quick review?
strings.in.hidden.d: About {amount} every month. Add it as a bill so Penny can forecast it.
strings.in.weekend.d: {pct} of your everyday spending happens on weekends.
strings.in.round.d: Rounding up {n} purchases last month adds up to about {year} a year.
strings.in.noMerchants: Add payees to your transactions to see where you spend most.
strings.in.noSpend: No spending in this range yet.
strings.in.tapBar: Click a month to see it
strings.in.wi.title: What if I spent less?
strings.in.wi.pick: Pick one or more categories (average a month):
strings.in.wi.empty: After a month of spending, try trimming categories here.
strings.in.wc.title: What changed?
strings.in.wc.sub: Biggest differences in {now} vs the same stretch before.
strings.in.wi.goal_one: You’d reach {name} {count} month sooner (in about {after} months).
strings.in.wi.goal_other: You’d reach {name} {count} months sooner (in about {after} months).
strings.in.wi.goalNew_one: That alone would reach {name} in about {count} month.
strings.in.wi.goalNew_other: That alone would reach {name} in about {count} months.
strings.goal.addCardD: A trip, a car, a safety net…
strings.set.themeD2: Penny’s two looks: Cream and Ink, or Night and Cream

strings.cm.title: Join the Penny community
strings.cm.long: Get help, share ideas and hear about new versions first, on our Discord server.
strings.cm.join: Join the Penny community on Discord
strings.cm.hidden: Hidden. You can join any time from Settings › Updates & help.

strings.att.addHint: Photos, PDFs or documents · drop them here or paste a screenshot
strings.att.err.TYPE: That kind of file can’t be attached. Use a photo, PDF or document.
strings.att.err.SIZE: That file is larger than 20 MB.
strings.att.err.MISSING: This file isn’t on this PC any more.
